notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • A disaster is a serious disruption caused when a hazardous event interacts with exposed and vulnerable people, assets or systems and produces major human, economic, material or environmental losses.
  • A hazard by itself does not automatically become a disaster. Exposure, vulnerability and coping capacity determine the scale of disaster risk.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hazard + Exposure + Vulnerability → Disaster Risk

2. Hazard
  • A hazard is a potentially damaging physical event, phenomenon or human activity.
  • Examples include:
  • Earthquake.
  • Cyclone.
  • Flood.
  • Landslide.
  • Drought.
  • Industrial accident.
3. Disaster Risk
  • Disaster risk represents the potential losses that may occur because a hazard affects exposed and vulnerable people or assets.
  • Risk increases when hazard, exposure and vulnerability are high and coping capacity is low.
4. Exposure
  • Exposure refers to people, houses, infrastructure, economic activities and other assets located in hazard-prone areas.
  • A powerful cyclone crossing an uninhabited coast may cause less disaster loss than a weaker cyclone striking a densely populated coastal city.
5. Vulnerability
  • Vulnerability refers to conditions that make people or assets more susceptible to damage.
  • Examples include:
  • Weak buildings.
  • Poverty.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Settlement on unstable slopes.
  • Lack of warning systems.
6. Capacity
  • Capacity means the strengths and resources available to anticipate, withstand, respond to and recover from disasters.
  • It includes:
  • Trained personnel.
  • Strong infrastructure.
  • Early warning.
  • Community knowledge.
  • Emergency services.
7. Resilience
  • Disaster resilience is the ability of individuals, communities and systems to resist, absorb, adapt to and recover from hazardous events.
  • Resilience is strengthened by preparedness, mitigation and risk-informed development.
8. Types of Disasters

Disasters may broadly arise from:

  • Geological hazards.
  • Hydrological hazards.
  • Meteorological hazards.
  • Climatological hazards.
  • Biological hazards.
  • Technological or human-induced hazards.
9. Geological Hazards

Examples include:

  • Earthquakes.
  • Landslides.
  • Volcanic eruptions.
  • Tsunamis generated by submarine geological disturbances.
10. Hydro-Meteorological Hazards

Important examples include:

  • Floods.
  • Cyclones.
  • Storm surges.
  • Cloudbursts.
  • Droughts.
  • Heat waves.
  • Lightning.

India faces substantial exposure to several of these hazards.

11. Human-Induced Disasters

Examples include:

  • Industrial accidents.
  • Chemical leaks.
  • Fires.
  • Nuclear and radiological accidents.
  • Transport accidents.
  • Dam failures.

Disaster management therefore covers both natural and human-induced hazards.

12. Disaster Management Cycle

Major stages include:

  • Prevention.
  • Mitigation.
  • Preparedness.
  • Response.
  • Relief.
  • Recovery.
  • Rehabilitation.
  • Reconstruction.

India's NDMA explicitly emphasises prevention, mitigation, preparedness and response, with recovery and rehabilitation forming part of the wider disaster-management framework.

13. Prevention
  • Prevention aims to avoid creation of disaster risk where possible.
  • Examples include:
  • Avoiding construction in highly hazardous zones.
  • Protecting natural drainage.
  • Enforcing safety standards.
14. Mitigation
  • Mitigation means reducing the severity of potential disaster impacts.
  • Examples include:
  • Earthquake-resistant construction.
  • Cyclone shelters.
  • Flood embankments.
  • Landslide slope stabilisation.
15. Preparedness

Preparedness includes:

  • Emergency plans.
  • Mock drills.
  • Evacuation routes.
  • Emergency supplies.
  • Warning systems.
  • Training.
16. Response

Response begins during or immediately after a disaster.

It includes:

  • Search and rescue.
  • Medical aid.
  • Evacuation.
  • Temporary shelter.
  • Emergency communication.
  • Relief distribution.
17. Recovery
  • Recovery restores normal social and economic functioning.
  • It may continue for months or years after a major disaster.
18. Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation may include:

  • Restoring livelihoods.
  • Repairing basic services.
  • Temporary-to-permanent housing transition.
  • Psychosocial support.
19. Reconstruction
  • Reconstruction involves rebuilding damaged infrastructure and settlements.
  • Modern disaster management emphasises rebuilding them more safely rather than reproducing the earlier vulnerability.
20. Build Back Better
  • "Build Back Better" means using recovery and reconstruction to increase future resilience.
  • It is one of the major ideas in the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Build Back Better → Safer Post-Disaster Reconstruction

21. Earthquake
  • An earthquake is sudden shaking of the ground caused by release of energy within Earth's crust.
  • Most damaging Indian earthquakes are tectonic in origin.
22. Focus / Hypocentre
  • The focus or hypocentre is the point inside Earth where an earthquake rupture begins.
23. Epicentre
  • The epicentre is the point on Earth's surface vertically above the focus.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Focus → Inside Earth

Epicentre → Surface

24. Seismic Waves

Major earthquake-wave groups are:

  • Body waves.
  • Surface waves.

Body waves include:

  • P waves.
  • S waves.
25. P Waves
  • P waves are primary waves.
  • They are the fastest seismic waves.
  • They can travel through:
  • Solids.
  • Liquids.
  • Gases.
26. S Waves
  • S waves are secondary waves.
  • They travel more slowly than P waves.
  • They cannot travel through liquids.
📌 Must-Memorise

P Wave → Solid + Liquid

S Wave → Solid Only

27. Surface Waves
  • Surface waves travel along Earth's surface.
  • They can produce severe shaking and structural damage.
28. Magnitude
  • Earthquake magnitude represents the energy released by an earthquake.
  • Modern seismology commonly uses moment magnitude for large earthquakes.
29. Intensity
  • Intensity describes the observed effects and damage caused by an earthquake at a particular location.
  • Intensity can differ from place to place for the same earthquake.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Magnitude → Earthquake Energy

Intensity → Effects at a Place

30. India's Seismic Zones

India's current conventional seismic zoning contains:

  • Zone II.
  • Zone III.
  • Zone IV.
  • Zone V.

Zone V represents the highest hazard category in this zoning system. NDMA states that a large part of India is exposed to moderate-to-severe seismic hazard.

📌 Must-Memorise

India Seismic Zones → II, III, IV, V

Highest → Zone V

31. Earthquake-Prone Regions of India

High seismic hazard occurs especially in:

  • Himalayan region.
  • Northeastern India.
  • Parts of Kachchh.
  • Andaman and Nicobar region.

The Himalayan hazard is closely related to continuing convergence of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

32. Himalayan Earthquakes
  • The Indian Plate continues moving toward the Eurasian Plate.
  • Stress accumulation and fault movement make the Himalayan belt highly earthquake-prone.
33. Earthquake Safety

Important measures include:

  • Earthquake-resistant design.
  • Building-code compliance.
  • Retrofitting vulnerable buildings.
  • Avoiding weak construction.
  • Securing heavy indoor objects.

NDMA's earthquake-risk programmes emphasise earthquake-resistant construction and safer building practices.

34. Retrofitting
  • Retrofitting means strengthening an existing building to improve its resistance to hazards such as earthquakes.
35. Earthquake Prediction
  • Exact prediction of the time, place and magnitude of a future earthquake remains extremely difficult.
  • Risk reduction therefore focuses heavily on preparedness and structural safety.
36. Liquefaction
  • Liquefaction occurs when loose, water-saturated sediments lose strength during intense shaking.
  • Buildings may tilt or sink where liquefaction occurs.
37. Tsunami
  • A tsunami is a series of long ocean waves generated by sudden displacement of a large volume of seawater.
  • Major causes include:
  • Submarine earthquakes.
  • Underwater landslides.
  • Volcanic activity.
38. Tsunami vs Ordinary Sea Wave
  • Tsunamis have very long wavelengths.
  • In deep ocean they may travel rapidly with relatively small wave height.
  • Near shallow coasts, wave height can increase dramatically.
39. Tsunami Generation

A submarine earthquake is most likely to generate a major tsunami when it causes significant vertical displacement of the seafloor.

40. Tsunami Warning in India
  • India's national tsunami advisories are issued by the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
  • The system uses seismic stations, tsunami buoys/bottom-pressure recorders, tide gauges and continuous monitoring.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tsunami Warning → INCOIS → Hyderabad

41. Indian Tsunami Early Warning System
  • The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre became operational after the catastrophic 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
  • INCOIS states that the warning centre has been operational since October 2007.
42. Tsunami Natural Warning Signs

People near a coast should recognise signs such as:

  • Strong or prolonged earthquake shaking.
  • Sudden unusual withdrawal of seawater.
  • Unusual roaring from the sea.

Immediate movement toward higher ground can be life-saving.

43. Cyclone
  • A tropical cyclone is an intense rotating low-pressure weather system.
  • It can produce three major destructive hazards:
  • Strong winds.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Storm surge.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cyclone Hazards → Wind + Rain + Storm Surge

44. North Indian Ocean Cyclone Basins

Cyclones affecting India develop mainly over:

  • Bay of Bengal.
  • Arabian Sea.
45. Cyclone Seasons

IMD identifies May-June and October-November as important periods for severe cyclonic activity over the North Indian Ocean, with the post-monsoon season particularly significant.

46. Cyclone Classification — IMD

IMD's wind-based categories include:

  • Depression → 31–49 km/h.
  • Deep Depression → 50–61 km/h.
  • Cyclonic Storm → 62–88 km/h.
  • Severe Cyclonic Storm → 89–117 km/h.
  • Very Severe Cyclonic Storm → 118–166 km/h.
  • Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm → 167–221 km/h.
  • Super Cyclonic Storm → 222 km/h or more.
📌 TNPSC Must-Memorise

Cyclonic Storm Begins → 62 km/h

47. Cyclone Landfall
  • Landfall occurs when the centre of a tropical cyclone crosses the coastline.
  • Strong winds, storm surge and heavy rainfall make the landfall period especially dangerous.
48. Eye of Cyclone
  • The eye is the relatively calm central region of a mature intense cyclone.
  • The strongest winds occur around the eyewall rather than at the exact centre.
49. Storm Surge
  • Storm surge is abnormal rise of sea level caused mainly by cyclone winds and low atmospheric pressure.
  • Surge impact can become worse when landfall coincides with high tide and where coastal waters are shallow.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Storm Surge ≠ Tsunami

50. Bay of Bengal Cyclone Risk

India's eastern coast is highly exposed to tropical cyclones originating over the Bay of Bengal.

Important vulnerable coastal states include:

  • Odisha.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • West Bengal.

IMD maintains cyclone-hazard climatology for Indian coastal districts.

51. Tamil Nadu Cyclone Risk

Tamil Nadu's Coromandel Coast is particularly vulnerable during the northeast-monsoon and post-monsoon cyclone season.

High-risk coastal districts include portions of:

  • Chennai region.
  • Cuddalore coast.
  • Nagapattinam coast.
  • Mayiladuthurai coast.
  • Ramanathapuram and adjoining coastal belts.
52. Cyclone Mitigation

Important measures include:

  • Accurate forecasting.
  • Early warning.
  • Cyclone shelters.
  • Evacuation.
  • Strong housing.
  • Coastal shelterbelts.
  • Emergency communication.
53. Doppler Weather Radar
  • Doppler Weather Radar helps monitor rainfall, storm structure and wind movement.
  • IMD uses DWR information in cyclone monitoring and forecasting.
📌 Must-Memorise

DWR → Cyclone / Severe Weather Monitoring

54. Flood
  • A flood occurs when water inundates normally dry land.
  • Causes include:
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • River overflow.
  • Cyclones.
  • Dam releases.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Snowmelt in some regions.
55. River Flood
  • River floods occur when river discharge exceeds channel capacity.
  • The Ganga-Brahmaputra plains are especially flood-prone.
56. Flash Flood
  • A flash flood develops rapidly, often after intense rainfall over a short period.
  • Mountain valleys and small catchments are particularly vulnerable.
57. Urban Flood

Urban flooding is intensified by:

  • Impervious surfaces.
  • Blocked drains.
  • Wetland loss.
  • Encroachment on waterways.
  • Extreme rainfall.
58. Coastal Flood

Coastal flooding can arise from:

  • Storm surge.
  • High tide.
  • Cyclones.
  • Tsunamis.
  • Sea-level rise.
59. Flood Forecasting in India
  • The Central Water Commission monitors flood situations and issues flood forecasts and advance warnings through its forecasting network.
📌 Must-Memorise

River Flood Forecasting → CWC

60. Flood Mitigation — Structural Measures

Examples include:

  • Dams.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Embankments.
  • Levees.
  • Drainage channels.
  • Diversion structures.
61. Flood Mitigation — Non-Structural Measures

Examples include:

  • Flood forecasting.
  • Floodplain zoning.
  • Land-use regulation.
  • Evacuation plans.
  • Insurance.
  • Community awareness.
62. Floodplain
  • A floodplain is relatively flat land beside a river that is naturally subject to flooding.
  • Occupying active floodplains increases exposure to flood hazards.
63. Wetlands and Flood Reduction
  • Wetlands temporarily store water and reduce peak runoff.
  • Destruction of urban wetlands can therefore worsen flood risk.
64. Drought
  • Drought is a prolonged period of water deficiency.
  • It differs from aridity, which is a long-term climatic characteristic.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Drought → Temporary/Abnormal Deficiency

Aridity → Long-Term Climatic Condition

65. Types of Drought

Important types include:

  • Meteorological drought.
  • Agricultural drought.
  • Hydrological drought.
  • Socioeconomic drought.
66. Meteorological Drought
  • Meteorological drought refers to substantial rainfall deficiency compared with normal climatic conditions.
67. Agricultural Drought
  • Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop requirements.
68. Hydrological Drought

Hydrological drought involves reduced:

  • River flow.
  • Reservoir storage.
  • Lake levels.
  • Groundwater availability.
69. Drought-Prone Regions

Drought risk is high in parts of:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Interior Tamil Nadu.
70. Drought Management

Important measures include:

  • Rainwater harvesting.
  • Watershed development.
  • Drought-tolerant crops.
  • Micro-irrigation.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Crop diversification.
71. Landslide
  • A landslide is downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity.
  • Landslide risk is influenced by geology, slope, rainfall and human disturbance.

The Geological Survey of India operates landslide-hazard and forecasting services.

72. Causes of Landslides

Natural triggers include:

  • Intense rainfall.
  • Earthquakes.
  • River erosion.
  • Weathering.

Human factors include:

  • Road cutting.
  • Quarrying.
  • Deforestation.
  • Poor slope drainage.
73. Landslide-Prone Regions

Important Indian landslide regions include:

  • Himalayas.
  • Northeastern hills.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Nilgiris.
74. Landslide Mitigation

Measures include:

  • Retaining walls.
  • Slope drainage.
  • Rock bolting.
  • Vegetation.
  • Controlled road cutting.
  • Hazard zonation.
  • Avoiding construction on unstable slopes.
75. Nilgiris Landslide Risk
  • Steep terrain, intense rainfall, road cutting and land-use changes make parts of the Nilgiris vulnerable to landslides.
  • Hazard-sensitive hill development is therefore important.
76. Avalanche
  • An avalanche is rapid downslope movement of snow and ice.
  • It is mainly a hazard of high Himalayan regions.
77. Cloudburst
  • A cloudburst is an extremely intense localised rainfall event over a short period.
  • It can trigger:
  • Flash floods.
  • Landslides.
  • Debris flows.
78. Heat Wave
  • A heat wave is a period of abnormally high temperature relative to local climatology.
  • India's official criteria depend on actual maximum temperature and departure from normal. NDMA currently notes that heat-wave consideration begins only after maximum temperature reaches at least 40°C in plains and 30°C in hilly regions, with additional IMD criteria applied thereafter.
79. Heat-Wave Impacts

Heat waves can cause:

  • Heat exhaustion.
  • Heat stroke.
  • Dehydration.
  • Higher electricity demand.
  • Crop stress.
  • Livestock mortality.
80. Heat-Wave Preparedness

NDMA advises measures including:

  • Maintaining hydration.
  • Avoiding peak afternoon sun.
  • Wearing light-coloured loose clothing.
  • Using shade and cooling measures.
  • Following official weather warnings.
81. Lightning
  • Lightning is a sudden electrical discharge in the atmosphere.
  • Thunderstorms can produce:
  • Lightning.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Strong winds.
  • Hail.
82. Lightning Safety

During lightning:

  • Avoid open fields.
  • Avoid isolated tall trees.
  • Move into a substantial building or safe vehicle.
  • Avoid contact with electrical systems and exposed metal where possible.
83. Forest Fire

Forest fires may be caused by:

  • Lightning.
  • Agricultural burning.
  • Careless human activity.
  • Deliberate ignition.
  • Dry vegetation combined with heat and wind.
84. Forest-Fire Management

Measures include:

  • Fire lines.
  • Early detection.
  • Fuel management.
  • Community surveillance.
  • Rapid-response teams.
  • Satellite monitoring.
85. Biological Disaster

Biological disasters include large-scale impacts from:

  • Epidemics.
  • Pandemics.
  • Animal diseases.
  • Plant diseases.
  • Biological agents.

Disaster-management frameworks therefore extend beyond purely physical hazards.

86. Industrial Disaster

Industrial disasters may involve:

  • Toxic chemical release.
  • Explosion.
  • Fire.
  • Structural failure.

Industrial areas need emergency-response plans and hazardous-material management.

87. Chemical Disaster

Chemical disasters can occur during:

  • Manufacture.
  • Storage.
  • Transportation.
  • Use of hazardous substances.
88. Nuclear and Radiological Emergency

These emergencies may arise from:

  • Nuclear facilities.
  • Radiation sources.
  • Transportation incidents.
  • Improper radioactive-material handling.

Specialised response capability forms part of India's disaster-response system.

89. Dam Failure

Dam failure can produce sudden downstream flooding.

Risk reduction requires:

  • Structural inspection.
  • Reservoir management.
  • Emergency action plans.
  • Downstream warning systems.
90. Disaster Management Act, 2005
  • The Disaster Management Act, 2005 created India's principal statutory framework for disaster management.
  • The Act is Act No. 53 of 2005 and was enacted on 23 December 2005.
📌 Must-Memorise

Disaster Management Act → 2005

91. National Disaster Management Authority
  • NDMA is India's apex disaster-management authority.
  • It is chaired by the Prime Minister of India.
  • It lays down policies, plans and guidelines for disaster management.
📌 Must-Memorise

NDMA Chairperson → Prime Minister

92. State Disaster Management Authority
  • The Disaster Management framework provides for authorities at state level.
  • State authorities coordinate disaster-management planning and implementation within their states.
93. District Disaster Management
  • Disaster-management institutions also operate at district level under the statutory framework.
  • District administration is crucial for:
  • Preparedness.
  • Evacuation.
  • Response.
  • Relief.
94. National Disaster Response Force
  • NDRF is the specialised national force for response to threatening disaster situations and disasters.
  • Section 44 of the Disaster Management Act provides for the National Disaster Response Force.
📌 Must-Memorise

NDRF → Specialist Disaster Response

95. NDRF Raising
  • The National Disaster Response Force was raised in January 2006 following enactment of the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
96. NDRF vs NDMA

NDMA:

  • Policy, planning and guidelines.

NDRF:

  • Specialised operational disaster response.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NDMA ≠ NDRF

97. National Institute of Disaster Management
  • NIDM supports disaster-management training, research, documentation and capacity building under the Disaster Management framework.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NIDM → Training + Research

98. Ministry of Home Affairs
  • Disaster management at the Union level is coordinated through the Ministry of Home Affairs along with specialised institutions and hazard-specific technical agencies.
99. Primary Responsibility of States
  • The Government of India states that primary responsibility for disaster management, including ground-level relief and response, rests with the state government concerned.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ground-Level Disaster Management → State Government Primary Responsibility

100. Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 — Current Exam Update
  • The Disaster Management Act was amended in 2025.
  • The Amendment Act was notified on 29 March 2025 and brought into force from 9 April 2025.
📌 Must-Memorise

DM Amendment → 2025

101. National Disaster Database — 2025 Amendment
  • The 2025 amendment mandates a National Disaster Database.
  • Official information says it includes disaster-risk assessment, mitigation plans and disaster-related data.
102. Urban Disaster Management Authority
  • The 2025 amendment added an enabling provision for states to constitute Urban Disaster Management Authorities in state capitals and cities with municipal corporations, subject to statutory exceptions.
  • These authorities are intended to address urban-specific hazards such as flooding and heat waves.
🔗 TNPSC Current-Affairs Link

UDMA → Added Through 2025 Amendment

103. High-Level Committee
  • The 2025 amendment gave statutory status to the High-Level Committee involved in disaster-management financing decisions.
104. Early Warning
  • Early warning combines:
  • Hazard detection.
  • Forecasting.
  • Communication.
  • Timely action.
  • A warning is effective only when people receive, understand and act on it.
105. Major Indian Warning Agencies

High-yield pairings include:

  • Cyclones and severe weather → IMD.
  • River floods → Central Water Commission.
  • Tsunami → INCOIS / Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre.
  • Landslide forecasting → Geological Survey of India.
106. IMD
  • India Meteorological Department monitors and forecasts:
  • Cyclones.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Heat waves.
  • Severe weather.
  • It operates the Regional Specialized Meteorological Centre for tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean.
107. CWC
  • Central Water Commission operates flood forecasting and hydrological observation services.
  • It issues flood forecasts and warnings to relevant agencies.
108. INCOIS
  • Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad.
109. GSI
  • Geological Survey of India provides landslide-hazard information and operates landslide-forecasting services.
110. SACHET
  • NDMA's SACHET platform provides geo-targeted disaster and weather alerts to citizens.
  • NDMA lists hazards such as floods, cyclones, landslides and earthquakes among the alerts distributed through the system.
111. Structural Measures

Structural disaster-mitigation measures include:

  • Cyclone shelters.
  • Earthquake-resistant buildings.
  • Embankments.
  • Retaining walls.
  • Storm-water drains.
112. Non-Structural Measures

Non-structural measures include:

  • Hazard maps.
  • Building regulations.
  • Land-use planning.
  • Insurance.
  • Awareness.
  • Early warning.
  • Evacuation plans.
113. Hazard Zonation
  • Hazard zonation divides an area according to the level of hazard.
  • It assists:
  • Land-use planning.
  • Infrastructure design.
  • Emergency planning.
114. Vulnerability Mapping

Vulnerability maps may identify:

  • Poor-quality housing.
  • High population density.
  • Critical infrastructure.
  • Elderly populations.
  • Hazard-exposed communities.
115. Risk Mapping

Risk mapping integrates information on:

  • Hazard.
  • Exposure.
  • Vulnerability.
  • Capacity.

This risk-based approach is consistent with modern disaster-risk-reduction frameworks.

116. Evacuation
  • Evacuation means moving people from a dangerous location to a safer area before or during an emergency.
  • Cyclone and tsunami evacuation should move people away from exposed coastal zones.
117. Emergency Operations Centre
  • An Emergency Operations Centre coordinates:
  • Information.
  • Agencies.
  • Resources.
  • Communication.
  • Response decisions.
118. Mock Drill
  • A mock drill simulates an emergency.
  • It tests:
  • Preparedness.
  • Evacuation.
  • Coordination.
  • Communication.
119. Search and Rescue

Search and rescue aims to:

  • Locate trapped persons.
  • Safely extract victims.
  • Provide immediate medical assistance.

NDRF is specifically organised for specialised disaster response.

120. Incident Response

Effective disaster response requires clear:

  • Command.
  • Coordination.
  • Communication.
  • Resource allocation.
121. Community-Based Disaster Management

Local communities are often the first affected and first to respond.

Community preparedness can include:

  • Local hazard maps.
  • Volunteer teams.
  • First-aid training.
  • Evacuation drills.
122. School Disaster Management

Schools should have:

  • Safe evacuation routes.
  • Assembly points.
  • Fire safety.
  • Earthquake drills where appropriate.
  • Emergency contact systems.
123. Hospital Preparedness

Hospitals need:

  • Backup electricity.
  • Emergency water.
  • Structural safety.
  • Mass-casualty plans.
  • Communication systems.
124. Critical Infrastructure

Critical infrastructure includes:

  • Hospitals.
  • Electricity.
  • Water systems.
  • Telecommunications.
  • Transport.
  • Emergency services.

Their failure can multiply disaster impacts.

125. Disaster Risk Reduction
  • Disaster Risk Reduction, or DRR, aims to prevent new risk and reduce existing risk.
  • It focuses on understanding hazards, vulnerability, exposure and resilience rather than only providing post-disaster relief.
📌 Must-Memorise

DRR → Reduce Disaster Risk Before Disaster Occurs

126. Sendai Framework
  • The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction covers 2015–2030.
  • It contains seven global targets and four priorities for action.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sendai Framework → 2015–2030

127. Four Sendai Priorities

The four priorities are:

1. Understanding disaster risk.

2. Strengthening disaster-risk governance.

3. Investing in disaster-risk reduction for resilience.

4. Enhancing preparedness for effective response and Build Back Better in recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

128. Disaster and Sustainable Development
  • Poorly planned development can create new disaster risk.
  • Risk-sensitive infrastructure and land-use planning improve long-term development resilience.
129. Climate Change and Disasters

Climate change can influence several hazards by affecting:

  • Extreme heat.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Drought conditions.
  • Coastal flooding.
  • Sea-level-related risks.

Detailed climate-change geography belongs to Chapter 26.

130. Tamil Nadu — Major Disaster Hazards

Tamil Nadu is exposed to multiple hazards including:

  • Tropical cyclones.
  • Coastal flooding and storm surge.
  • Tsunami.
  • Drought.
  • Urban floods.
  • Heat waves.
  • Landslides in hill regions.

Its long Bay of Bengal-facing coastline makes coastal preparedness particularly important.

131. Coromandel Coast Hazard
  • The Coromandel Coast is particularly exposed to Bay of Bengal cyclones during the post-monsoon/northeast-monsoon period.
  • Cyclone hazards include wind, rainfall and storm surge.
132. Chennai Flood Risk

Chennai's flood risk is influenced by:

  • Intense northeast-monsoon rainfall.
  • Low-lying coastal terrain.
  • Rivers and drainage channels.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Reduced natural water-storage areas.
133. Chennai Coastal Hazards

Chennai faces risks from:

  • Cyclones.
  • Storm surge.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Urban flooding.

Its location on the Bay of Bengal coast makes multi-hazard planning essential.

134. Tamil Nadu Tsunami Risk
  • Tamil Nadu is vulnerable to Indian Ocean tsunami hazards because of its long southeast-facing coastline.
  • Tsunami warnings for the coast are provided through India's INCOIS-operated warning system.
135. Nilgiris Hazard

Nilgiris faces:

  • Landslides.
  • Intense rainfall.
  • Slope instability.

Safe road cutting, drainage and controlled hill construction are essential.

136. Western Ghats Hazard

Western Ghats districts may face:

  • Landslides.
  • Flash floods.
  • Intense rainfall.
  • Forest fires during dry periods.
137. Tamil Nadu Drought Risk

Interior districts are vulnerable where:

  • Rainfall is low or variable.
  • Tanks fail to fill.
  • Groundwater is overused.
  • Monsoon rainfall fails.
138. Tank Systems and Disaster Reduction

Tamil Nadu tanks can help:

  • Store intense rainfall.
  • Moderate local runoff.
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Provide drought storage.

Protecting tank catchments and surplus channels therefore supports both flood and drought resilience.

139. Wetlands and Chennai Resilience

Wetlands and natural drainage areas provide:

  • Temporary flood storage.
  • Runoff moderation.
  • Ecological functions.

Urban encroachment can reduce these benefits.

140. Coastal Mangroves and Disaster Risk

Mangroves can:

  • Reduce wave energy.
  • Stabilise sediments.
  • Provide a natural coastal buffer.

They supplement but do not replace engineered evacuation and disaster-safety measures.

141. Pichavaram and Muthupet
  • Pichavaram and Muthupet are important Tamil Nadu mangrove systems.
  • Conserving such coastal ecosystems contributes to broader coastal resilience.
142. Disaster Preparedness for Fishermen

Important measures include:

  • IMD marine weather warnings.
  • Cyclone alerts.
  • Reliable communication.
  • Avoiding sea travel during severe warnings.
  • Safe harbour access.

IMD issues marine and cyclone forecast products including wind, wave and storm-surge information.

143. Urban Heat Risk in Tamil Nadu

Dense cities can experience greater heat stress because of:

  • Built surfaces.
  • Limited vegetation.
  • High night-time temperatures.
  • Urban heat-island effects.

Heat Action Plans, hydration, shade and public warnings reduce risk.

144. Disaster-Resilient Construction

Construction should consider local hazards:

  • Earthquake zone.
  • Flood level.
  • Cyclone wind.
  • Landslide susceptibility.
  • Coastal erosion.
145. Land-Use Planning

Avoiding construction in:

  • Active floodplains.
  • Unstable slopes.
  • Natural drainage channels.
  • Highly exposed coastal strips.

can significantly reduce future exposure.

146. Nature-Based Solutions

Natural systems can contribute to disaster-risk reduction.

Examples include:

  • Mangrove restoration.
  • Wetland conservation.
  • Forest restoration.
  • Watershed treatment.
147. Technology in Disaster Management

Important technologies include:

  • Satellites.
  • Doppler radar.
  • GIS.
  • GPS.
  • Weather models.
  • River gauges.
  • Seismic networks.
  • Tsunami buoys.

India's cyclone, flood, tsunami and landslide warning systems make extensive use of these technologies.

148. GIS

GIS is useful for:

  • Hazard mapping.
  • Evacuation planning.
  • Relief distribution.
  • Damage assessment.
149. Remote Sensing

Satellite remote sensing can support:

  • Flood mapping.
  • Cyclone monitoring.
  • Landslide assessment.
  • Drought assessment.
  • Forest-fire monitoring.
150. Early Warning to Early Action
  • Forecasting alone cannot prevent disaster losses.
  • Warnings must reach exposed communities in time and trigger appropriate protective action.

This reflects the broader risk-reduction approach promoted by NDMA and the Sendai Framework.

154. TNPSC Traps
  • Hazard and disaster are not the same.
  • High hazard does not automatically mean high disaster loss.
  • Exposure and vulnerability are critical components of risk.
  • Mitigation occurs mainly before a disaster.
  • Response is not the whole of disaster management.
  • Focus and epicentre are different.
  • P waves pass through liquids; S waves do not.
  • Magnitude and intensity are different.
  • India's seismic zones are II, III, IV and V.
  • Zone V represents the highest seismic hazard category.
  • Tsunami and storm surge are different.
  • Cyclone landfall means the cyclone's centre crosses the coast.
  • Strongest cyclone winds are concentrated around the eyewall.
  • IMD's Cyclonic Storm category begins at 62 km/h.
  • Cyclone's three major hazards are wind, rain and storm surge.
  • Drought and aridity are different.
  • Flash floods develop rapidly.
  • Urban flooding is strongly influenced by drainage and land use.
  • CWC handles river-flood forecasting.
  • INCOIS issues India's tsunami advisories.
  • GSI handles landslide-hazard/forecasting functions.
  • NDMA and NDRF are different.
  • NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister.
  • NDRF provides specialised response.
  • Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2005.
  • The Disaster Management Act was amended in 2025.
  • Sendai Framework runs from 2015 to 2030.
  • Build Back Better relates to recovery and reconstruction.

  • Exposure → In harm's way.
  • Vulnerability → Susceptibility.
  • Capacity → Ability to cope.
  • Risk → Hazard + exposure + vulnerability.
  • Focus → Inside.
  • Epicentre → Surface.
  • P wave → Solid + liquid.
  • S wave → Solid.
  • Zone V → Highest.
  • Cyclone → Wind + rain + surge.
  • CS → 62 km/h.
  • Flood warning → CWC.
  • Cyclone warning → IMD.
  • Tsunami → INCOIS.
  • Landslide → GSI.
  • NDMA → Policy.
  • NDRF → Response.
  • NIDM → Training.
  • DM Act → 2005.
  • Amendment → 2025.
  • Sendai → 2015–2030.
  • Build Back Better → Recovery.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is a disaster? → Serious disruption caused when a hazard interacts with exposure and vulnerability.
  • What is a hazard? → Potentially damaging event or process.
  • What is exposure? → People and assets located in hazard-prone areas.
  • What is vulnerability? → Susceptibility to damage.
  • What is capacity? → Ability to anticipate, cope and recover.
  • What is resilience? → Ability to withstand and recover from disasters.
  • Major disaster-management stages? → Prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.
  • What is mitigation? → Reducing potential disaster impact.
  • What is preparedness? → Planning and readiness before a disaster.
  • What is Build Back Better? → Reconstructing more safely after disaster.
  • What is earthquake focus? → Point inside Earth where rupture begins.
  • What is epicentre? → Surface point above the focus.
  • Fastest seismic wave? → P wave.
  • Which wave cannot pass through liquids? → S wave.
  • Magnitude measures? → Energy released.
  • Intensity measures? → Effects at a particular location.
  • How many conventional Indian seismic zones? → Four.
  • Name them. → II, III, IV and V.
  • Highest seismic zone? → Zone V.
  • Major Indian earthquake belt? → Himalayas and Northeast.
  • Main tectonic cause of Himalayan earthquakes? → Indian Plate-Eurasian Plate convergence.
  • What is liquefaction? → Loss of strength in water-saturated loose sediment during shaking.
  • What is a tsunami? → Series of long waves caused by sudden displacement of seawater.
  • India's tsunami-warning authority? → Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS.
  • INCOIS is located in? → Hyderabad.
  • Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre became operational in? → 2007.
  • What is a tropical cyclone? → Rotating intense low-pressure system over warm tropical ocean.
  • Three major cyclone hazards? → Strong winds, heavy rain and storm surge.
  • Cyclonic Storm wind-speed range under IMD? → 62–88 km/h.
  • Severe Cyclonic Storm? → 89–117 km/h.
  • Very Severe Cyclonic Storm? → 118–166 km/h.
  • Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm? → 167–221 km/h.
  • Super Cyclonic Storm? → 222 km/h or above.
  • What is cyclone landfall? → Crossing of the coast by the cyclone's centre.
  • What is storm surge? → Abnormal cyclone-driven rise in coastal sea level.
  • Is a storm surge a tsunami? → No.
  • Main Indian cyclone-warning agency? → IMD.
  • Which Indian coast is highly exposed to Bay of Bengal cyclones? → Eastern coast.
  • Which Tamil Nadu coast is highly cyclone-prone? → Coromandel Coast.
  • What is a flood? → Inundation of normally dry land.
  • What is a flash flood? → Rapid-onset flood.
  • What is urban flooding? → Flooding of built-up areas due to intense rainfall, drainage limitations and related factors.
  • Indian river-flood forecasting agency? → Central Water Commission.
  • What is a floodplain? → Flat land adjacent to a river naturally liable to flooding.
  • How do wetlands reduce floods? → They store and slow runoff.
  • What is drought? → Prolonged abnormal water deficiency.
  • Four important drought types? → Meteorological, agricultural, hydrological and socioeconomic.
  • What is agricultural drought? → Inadequate soil moisture for crops.
  • What is hydrological drought? → Reduced river, reservoir and groundwater availability.
  • What is a landslide? → Downslope movement of rock, soil or debris.
  • Major Indian landslide regions? → Himalayas, Northeast and Western Ghats.
  • Which national organisation deals with landslide forecasting? → Geological Survey of India.
  • Tamil Nadu region especially vulnerable to landslides? → Nilgiris.
  • What is an avalanche? → Rapid movement of snow and ice downslope.
  • What is a cloudburst? → Extremely intense localised rainfall over a short period.
  • What is a heat wave? → Abnormally high temperature relative to local climate.
  • What are structural mitigation measures? → Physical constructions such as shelters, embankments and resistant buildings.
  • What are non-structural measures? → Planning, warning, mapping, regulation and awareness.
  • Disaster Management Act enacted in? → 2005.
  • Act number? → Act No. 53 of 2005.
  • What is NDMA? → National Disaster Management Authority.
  • Who chairs NDMA? → Prime Minister of India.
  • What is NDRF? → National Disaster Response Force.
  • Main function of NDRF? → Specialised disaster response.
  • What is NIDM associated with? → Disaster-management training and research.
  • Which level has primary responsibility for ground-level disaster management? → State Government.
  • Which major Disaster Management law was amended in 2025? → Disaster Management Act, 2005.
  • When did the 2025 amendment come into force? → 9 April 2025.
  • What important database was mandated by the 2025 amendment? → National Disaster Database.
  • What urban institution was enabled by the 2025 amendment? → Urban Disaster Management Authority.
  • Sendai Framework period? → 2015–2030.
  • How many Sendai priorities? → Four.
  • First Sendai priority? → Understanding disaster risk.
  • Second? → Strengthening disaster-risk governance.
  • Third? → Investing in disaster-risk reduction for resilience.
  • Fourth? → Enhancing preparedness and Build Back Better.
  • Cyclone warning → Which agency? → IMD.
  • Flood forecasting → Which agency? → CWC.
  • Tsunami warning → Which agency? → INCOIS.
  • Landslide forecasting → Which agency? → GSI.
  • Why is Tamil Nadu disaster-prone? → Long cyclone-exposed coast, monsoon variability, drought-prone interiors, flood-prone cities and landslide-prone hill regions.
  • Which Tamil Nadu natural systems help reduce coastal hazard? → Mangroves and coastal wetlands.
  • Which Tamil Nadu traditional water systems assist both flood and drought management? → Eri/tank systems.
  • What is the most important shift in modern disaster management? → From relief-centred response toward prevention, risk reduction, preparedness and resilience.
